payload.title: The Night Shift of the Brain
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, sleep was treated as an empty space between the useful hours of the day. Doctors described it as a kind of switching off, and ambitious students were praised for getting by on four or five hours. The advice sounded sensible enough: if the brain does nothing while we sleep, then sleeping less should simply buy us more time.

Recording equipment changed that picture completely. Far from switching off, the sleeping brain turns out to be strikingly busy. During the deeper stages of the night it replays the electrical patterns of the day at high speed, moving fragile new memories from temporary storage into more permanent networks. At the same time, fluid washes through the tissue and carries away the waste proteins that build up during waking hours.

This is why a lost night costs more than it appears to. Volunteers kept awake for a single night remember far less of what they studied the day before, and they are noticeably worse at judging their own performance. The tired brain, in other words, loses the very tool it would need to notice how tired it is. Sleep is not the price we pay for the day; it is part of the work the day requires.

payload.title: The Box That Changed the World
paragraphs: Before the 1950s, loading a ship was slow and dangerous work. Barrels, sacks and wooden crates of every shape were carried aboard one by one by teams of dock workers, and a single vessel could sit in port for a week or more. Shipping cost so much that a factory rarely sold its goods far beyond its own region.

The solution was almost absurdly simple: a plain steel box of a fixed size that could be lifted straight from a truck onto a ship without anyone touching what was inside. Ports resisted at first, since the boxes demanded expensive new cranes and far fewer workers, and long strikes followed. Yet once a few harbours had rebuilt themselves, the others had little choice but to follow.

The consequences reached well beyond the docks. As the cost of moving goods collapsed, factories could be built wherever labour was cheapest rather than wherever customers happened to live, and shops filled with products assembled from parts made on three continents. A box with no moving parts and no clever technology inside it had quietly rearranged the map of world trade.
